utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good mornings, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I appear for the Prosecution together with my colleagues Mr. Hannis and Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence team of Mr. Mico Stanisic, it is Slobodan Cvijetic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And may the -- unless there is some reason to delay this, may the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Di Fazio to continue his cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- I remind you you're still on your oath. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, the very last topic that I want to discuss that's strictly from your report is the issue of your example of Bijeljina which I think you say indicates a systemic problem in the Prosecution's reports. And you deal well these -- this issue at paragraphs 233 and 234 of your report. I want to put a proposition to you, and please understand that I'm not interested in debating or quibbling with the figures. Let's proceed on the assumption that all of the figures that you have mentioned in paragraphs 233 and 234 are all correct, all the percentages and so on. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that about the figures. But, as I obtained these results, I proved that the results that were reached by Ewa Tabeau are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And are totally unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I understand that. I understand that. And we've heard your evidence. I think you indeed explained things again towards the end of your evidence the other day and it's here in your report as well. So I've heard what you have to say. And I don't want to debate the figures that have you in paragraphs 233 and 234. You say that the total population in 1991 that was born before 1980 is 81.650 or at least that's the figure that you chose from the Tabeau reports; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Then you say, and you look at the census figures, and the population, the whole population, entire population of Bijeljina was 96.988; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And so then you concluded that, well, if you look at 81.650, that's 84.18 per cent of 96.900-odd?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And if that's so, then the population up to 18 years of age must constitute about 26 per cent of the population. If that's so.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, according to the official results of the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, therefore, for whatever reason, I'm not interested in the reason, but for whatever reason, the figure of 15.82 per cent in the Tabeau reports is far too low; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the young contingent, up until the age of 18, and that is population that is under age and that is not registered as voters, that is a very low rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you perfectly and we understand each other. However, if you look at the group of people who in 1991 were aged 12, up to 12, that's a smaller group, isn't it? Let me rephrase it. If one were to look at the segment of the population between 1 and 12, that's a smaller group, isn't it? I'm sure you can answer that with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it's smaller, the group between 1 and 12, because it involves a smaller share of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In absolute terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Exactly. It doesn't include, 13 year olds, 14 year olds, 15 year olds, 16 year olds, 17 year olds, et cetera; right? Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a simple thing, isn't it, between zero and 12, whatever is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if you were aged 11 or 12 in -- 12 in 1991, by the time you got to 1997, you would have been eligible to vote, just, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the period when we use estimates for our calculations. And that is precisely what I dispute in my paper, and I'm prepared to prove that by using another example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that when you looked at the population of Bijeljina up to 18 years of age and concluded that the figure of 15.82 per cent was too low, you were looking at the wrong group. You should have been looking at people up to 12 years of age. That's the suggestion I make.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way we looked at it. May I suggest that you look at paragraph 253 and then it's going to be clearer. I provided a table there regarding the age structure of the population of the municipality of Bijeljina according to the 1991 census. These data show that the contingent of the young population up until the age of 18 accounts for a 26 per cent share. And it is 15 per cent in 1998. What I prove is that it is impossible over only five or six years to have the population change its age structure to such an extent. Such things are very rare anywhere in the world. That is what we know from demography. And it is impossible in this area. That is the result of my research and therefore I come to the conclusion that the estimated population in 1997 and 1998 that is born in 1980 is exaggerated because in Bijeljina the population was not so old. Rather, it was not people over 18. That is what we can prove using other examples too, which is what we discussed yesterday when we talked about the voters register of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 2.6 million people and the estimated population of 3.4 million. And when we match the two, on one example of Ewa Tabeau's, the share of the young population is about 24 per cent in BH as a whole, and in the example of Bijeljina, it is 15 per cent for the same period. That is absurd. That is simply impossible because if you look at the features of the population of Bijeljina, it is a proper sample for the processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You agree, though, that in 1991 you had to be at least 12 in order to be able to register to vote in 1997. That's -- you had to be at least that; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no dispute about the that. We agree. We have data to that effect, and we have estimates for 1998, when they became voters. That is precisely the figures that I'm challenging in Ewa Tabeau's report, that they were exaggerated in this case, if you look at the example of the municipality of Bijeljina. However, analogously, in view of the all of the other municipalities in this demographic survey, too, that is the case, because the population is fairly similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, I'm going to leave that topic now and I want to move on to another area. In your report, you warn against statistics involving - and I quote from paragraph 7 - "apocryphal numbers of the scope of criminal enterprises which are often exaggerated or minimised." Do you remember making that comment? Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the introductory part where I provide general comments. That paragraph 7 just intimates what I elaborated further in my report; namely, that in some examples, because these are estimates, in these cases we do not have fully and accurate figures. We have some exaggerated figures. For example, some organisations in Bosnia and Herzegovina reported that there were 200- or 300.000 persons killed. That is exaggerated. However, there are others that were minimised, which I show in the research of the demographic research of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. I just want to remind you, I'm not actually asking for any commentary. I will ask eventually, but I just want to remind you of things that you said in your report. At paragraph 229 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I go back for one moment to the -- to the previous line of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it your position that the 15-and-odd thousand number being the difference between the total population and 84-and-odd thousand. Yes? You see where I am?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The previous question --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- about the plus 12 and the minus 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The age segment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it your position that the 15-thousand-and-odd in Ewa Tabeau's report refer to only a part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- the 15 per cent mentioned in paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- the 15 per cent, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The 15 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is only a part of the group of minus 18 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. It's a smaller group. It's up to 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's up to 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought your point was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you -- perhaps I missed that, but did you confront the witness with the reasons why you think so?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I didn't because I understood from paragraph 234 that he was looking at a larger group. And when complaining about the 15 per cent figure being too low --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's too low, Professor Pasalic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And you say he's wrong because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The complaint is wrong because it's not up to -- it's not the group zero to 18, it's the group zero to 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where do you get that from? That's more or less my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Because it's inherent from the Tabeau's reports that she examined -- she compared two populations from the 1997 -- those eligible to vote, and in -- that meant that 1991 they had to be at least 12 years old, so she excluded those younger than 12 and compared those two populations, not those who were 18 or younger in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I think in paragraph -- I got to paragraph 229 in your report where you warn against manipulation of numbers. You say a number says whatever the person who can play with it wants. And I suppose I should get to my ultimate point which is to quote to you from paragraph 287, where you say, and perhaps you can look at that: "In this particular case of 18 municipalities from the Stanisic and Zupljanin indictment, a large number of objections regarding the number and structure of victims can be made. The data is based on estimations and unreliable sources and a biased research of war victims in BH." So you don't mention what sort of bias there, but essentially you're suggesting, aren't you, that the reports produced by Tabeau, in relation to population movements at least, is biased?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to look at all the other paragraphs as well, after which this conclusion follows. In this report, I did not elaborate on the victims in greater detail because I assumed and thought that this was more in the domain of other things that have to be proven in these proceedings. However, before paragraph 287, I indicated that numbers of victims were manipulated by certain institutions. Some said that there were even 300-, 400-, or 500.000 victims. That's what some organisations said. And then there was some more specific information that was provided by the institute from Sarajevo headed by Tokaca and that figure was 98.000. Then Ewa Tabeau's report appeared with a somewhat larger number of victims, 104.732. There are critical and self-critical reviews of the data involved. I spoke about that in great detail over the past few days. As for this conclusion in paragraph 287, it is derived from what I say in 286. I am indicating the book entitled "The Suffering of the Serbs in BH 1992-1995." That is my book. That is why I didn't elaborate on this any further. Yesterday we discussed these demographic processes in greater detail, or, rather, the destruction of the Serb population in the period from 1992 to 1995, and then that provides a more complete picture of all the victims of the war or of displaced persons and refugees. Now, why was this data study in a one-sided manner? As we've pointed out over the past few days -- please allow me to say this. It is important, please. If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any sample in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 20, 47, 15, whatever number of municipalities cannot provide a reliable picture of what happened in terms of the number of war victims and other demographic processes. If I may, as far as war victims are concerned, in the report of Ewa Tabeau the first thing that I believe is missing is the total population, even in this sample of municipalities, and then her qualification, her distinction, between the military and civilians. What does that number mean, of either one or the other, if you don't know what the phenomenon was if you look at it as a whole? What does 12.000 mean if you don't know the overall number of soldiers? Was it 50.000, 100.000, 150.000? Or if you look at civilian victims as well, it's the same. It is impossible to speak of structures or parts of a phenomenon without referring to the magnitude of the said phenomenon. That is what is lacking in this paper, and therefore it cannot be valid in research of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, I'm not, in the slightest, interested in going back to demographics and asking about statistics or particular aspects of the Tabeau reports at all. I'm asking you about the issue of accusations of bias. In paragraph 287, you make it clear. You say: "The data referring to the Tabeau reports is based on estimations and unreliable sources and a biased research of war victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" That is and acquisition of bias, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is biased because if we were to take a different example, then we would get a completely different picture of groups of victims, civilians and soldiers, so if we were to take a different municipality from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the picture would be different. That is why I'm challenging the sample that was taken that would provide relevant information about the number of civilians who were victims and soldiers who were victims. I say that what is relevant is only the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina where we can obtain valid, comprehensive data on the condition that all of this had been fully explored. However, I had some criticism in view of how that was done as well. If you wish, I can tell you now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if -- we can go back to the transcript, I think, and see what you said in court. On one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Mr. Pasalic, in my understanding, there's a difference between something being wrong or incorrect, on the one hand, and biased on the other. If something is wrong or incorrect, it could be because the author simply didn't understand the issue or made a mistake or something. To be biased is something completely different. That requires an intention to deliberately provide a picture which is designed to suit a certain perception of what happened. So do you -- are you saying that Ms. Tabeau had such a deliberate intent to disfigure the -- the data; and if so, why was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may assist. This is a terminological issue. If the English translation is "bias," then it's wrong. In our language, a one-sided research does not mean a -- is not the same as biased research. And in this sense, I believe the -- Professor Pasalic can elaborate. He interprets the word in the meaning it has in our language. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop you there, Mr. Cvijetic. I too was curious as to whether the word chosen by the translators of biased carried the connotations as the writer of the report intended that it does as an English word. And this is the point that Judge Harhoff was making. But the reason why I've stopped you is that I think you have crossed the line and are, yourself, giving evidence. It is an important issue, but it is something which the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- should address. So, Professor, you have Judge Harhoff's question before you, which you were in the process of answering, and perhaps it is something that Mr. Di Fazio may wish to explore. If you wish, Judge Harhoff could repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understood the question. I certainly do not think that Ewa Tabeau wanted to be biased. This is probably a translation issue. Incomplete, unreliable, one-sided research means that not all possible indicators were taken into account, or sources of data to lead such evidence. When you compare the number of victims, then you match the data about these victims. You take the census from 1991 and the data from some institution or from some register that this person was killed, and this data is not contested. But what about the victims of the war who were not registered in the census? And there were many in various military formations, such as some Mujahedin. It has been proven beyond doubt that they were present in the BH army. How do you match this data? And so on. That is why I think that this research is incomplete and that the establishment of the number of victims is a very complex process, that drawing conclusions from internal registers of some structures, mostly military, that were liable to manipulation of the victims, be it military or civilian, for some subjective reasons; for example, to get entitlement to some benefits for the families. And these numbers obtained by Ewa Tabeau by statistical means cannot be proven correct. This does not point toward her intention of bias. Of course, such errors would be much more dangerous than errors such as are made unintentionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the transcript from Wednesday, page 20575, you're talking about the methodological approach adopted by Ms. Tabeau. You said this: "The methodological approach adopted in the report of Ms. Tabeau and associates is mainly based on statistical and mathematical methods, that is, the law of numbers. This is insufficient for research of such complexity. After all, such a research is based on calculations by way of numbers. There is a maxime in statistical science saying that the number will tell you only so much as the person who plays with it wants you to know." Aren't you, there, suggesting that numbers were manipulated, or influenced at least, in such a way to present the picture that the authors wanted you to have, the -- Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I used a metaphor here that is used in statistics. The -- namely, that a number can do as much as the one willing to play with it. That doesn't mean that anybody played around with numbers intentionally. But based on the methods he or she used, they can arrive at very different results and a very differ picture of a process or phenomenon as compared to some other researchers that apply different methods. And I tried to illustrate that using some examples. Using different methods, on one hand only numbers and on the other hand combined research methods, we would arrive at different results, and that is not contested when it comes to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the war. We don't have final results for any of these phenomena yet. In Ewa Tabeau's report, the opinion is upheld that the estimated data is the most accurate and the most reliable of all. And that's where we differ. We would never -- I would never use only the statistical, mathematical method to prove these phenomena because we are talking about an area with its particularities with some processes that cannot reflected merely in numbers. That's why I used the metaphor that warns us all that a number by itself cannot provide an answer to such complex problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, Professor Pasalic, I suggest you're back-peddling now and that the combination of the excerpts from your reports and the transcript that I've quoted to you over the last few minutes indicate that you have been making or did make a -- level an accusation of bias against the authors of the -- against Tabeau and her papers. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I have never used the term "biased." But unreliability and reliability and one-sidedness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You mentioned in your testimony that you're a person who gladly accepts invitations to speak to the newspapers and to discuss matters of demographics in newspapers. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated as much. But I want to add that this is about contemporary demographic processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that from today's vantage point -- or, rather, this isn't about speaking about demographic processes during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina from today's vantage point. But, of course, it depends on the media, what they are interested in at any given moment. I consider it a professional duty of mine to respond to their invitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And before I proceed to the next line of questioning, there's one more thing I want to remind you about. And that is your -- you complained, didn't you, in your report, that the -- the Tabeau reports are characterised by certain dryness based on numbers. I may not disagree with you on the issue of dryness, but this is what you had to say: "The professional qualifications and the experiences of its authors indicate their orientation towards mathematical demography, quantitative methods, econometrics, and similar. It's noticeable that the authors, in keeping with their professional qualifications, mostly use methods based on dry numbers, samples, and other sources." Is that a complaint or not, that their approach is too dry, too mathematical?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my assessment of that survey, that report, where the authors, in line with their specialty as statistical demographers, and that is but one discipline in demography which is a broader whole, mostly applied that approach only. And when we discuss such complex processes, we cannot conduct complex research unless we use the methods of field research, empirical research. And these are missing from this report. I absolute stand by that. But I repeat: This is my assessment of their -- of the way they went about their research and the methods they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps I should get to the point and show you some newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 20086, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, the material -- the next document that I want to show you is an extract from a newspaper. And to make it clear, it was obtained from the Internet. I just want you to have a look and see -- look at this small article.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 20086.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's coming up on the screen I can ask you another question. You've been a politician since at least 1990, haven't you? You've been in various political parties, haven't you? In fact, you've held a position in the Republika Srpska government.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was active in politics. I said that until 1990 I was the last president of the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of the Zavidovici municipality. That was not a political party. It was considered a sort of people's front or something like that. The only party at the time was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. During the war I was not active in politics. Although -- or, rather, and I can add that I've never been a member of the Serb Democratic Party, which was the ruling party then. I guess that's what's behind your question. And now I'm a member of the party of Milorad Dodik. I don't have an executive position in the party. I was minister of education in 2001 until 2003 based on my professional merits. Now I'm a member of the Republican Council, which is an advisory body. I was its first president and now I'm a mere member. This is not a political body, I repeat. This is a professional body that gives advice to the government. And I'm a member of the Academy of Sciences and Arts of the Republika Srpska, which is an academic institution, not a political organisation. I stopped my political activity some time ago due to biological processes. I thought it was time to make room for younger people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could you look at the article on the screen. It's a short article from something called SRNA Review of Daily News from 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence complains. You know our position with regard to the use of newspaper articles as evidence. However, the Prosecution is going even further than that. This isn't even a newspaper article. This is a news item from a news agency where one sentence was taken out of context. I believe that goes beyond the limit that the Trial Chamber has allowed so far with regard to the use of complete articles. We believe that it would be fair to have the entire context of this interview or article where Professor Pasalic discussed something. I admit that in this -- even in this sentence taken out of context I see no problem, if it is reproduced correctly. But I believe that we have the right to demand -- to request to be shown the entire article. I think we have gone too far when it comes to using reports and articles from the mass media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, the -- essentially, Mr. Cvijetic has a point, doesn't he, in terms of the -- we all know the problems of the Internet, and the -- I suppose the -- whereas we can't ignore material that comes from that source, the way that -- it has to be treated in a way that isn't, in this case, unfair to the witness. So perhaps you can carefully phrase your question with all of those caveats in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can do that. And I also agree with Mr. Cvijetic; it would be preferable to have an entire article, if there was an entire article in existence or if it was available to me. But this is the best that the Prosecution can produce. It doesn't have any full article. I don't even know if there is a full article. But I'll proceed in the manner that you have outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will decide whether it will allow it or not. I would just like to remind everybody that there is a site on the Internet where you type in your name and you will get your own statements that you made at some time or another. I found on the Internet that I, as an attorney, stated something in a trial, although I've never even been in that trial. I don't know who uploads such things to the Internet. Certainly we cannot prevent them from doing so. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it would be too much to attribute --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- probative value to such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You have seen the article in front of you, and I think by now you must have had a chance to read it. Okay? Did you speak to a reporter around or on or before August 24 1996 on behalf of the democratic patriotic block concerning relationships with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, this was how long? 15, 16 years ago. I don't know why this would be an interview made up. But the democratic block also had some candidates that were not party members, and I believe that I was on a slate, on an election slate. The SRNA news agency only gives very short news items. And why did they reproduce my words? I was one of the few people who immediately after the war produced data about the suffering of the Serb population and Serb settlements in the territory of the Federation. And in that context, immediately after the war, there was discussion about the inter-entity boundary lines which were finally drawn in the Dayton Accord. But I see no problem with this. Even if we were to accept this at face value, and it's possible that I stated as much in a context, why should we pretend that we were brothers? We have never been brothers. We have always been neighbours. In Yugoslavia, there was this thing that was called a fraternity, but it burst like a soap bubble. I'm not putting forward any rigid positions toward another ethnic group. I'm merely stating the reality of the time. This has changed greatly in the meantime, though. 25.000 Bosniaks have returned to Bijeljina now. And we lived alongside them and we act together in local bodies and so on, so time remedies these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I take it that you said those words or words to the effect: "The aim of the DPB is that the boundary line between the two entities be finally defined. We can live with the Muslims as their neighbours, but not at all as their brothers ..." Now, did you say that, or words to that effect, to a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot possibly remember and quote myself after 15 years. That's an impossibility. But I believe that I did speak about these problems in this context, because I don't think the news agency would have made this up. But we must remember that journalists very often interpret people's words more freely, without understanding technical things. And that's what I always have in mind when I give interviews nowadays. Because if you always took the time to review your statement before it's printed, then you would never give an interview. Journalists always extract what seems most interesting to them, and that can create a one-sided or distorted picture of what you want to -- wanted to speak about. Newspaper articles are not reviewed. They are free interpretations. And there is certainly a public or moral responsibility, but I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, I think we can proceed on the basis that we all -- everyone here is well aware of problems inherent in journalism and the caution that must be adopted in dealing with -- with the media, okay? Let's proceed on that basis. But my simple question is: Did you say words, those words, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Di Fazio, hasn't he answered the question? You might not accept or agree with his explanation, but in the first part of his answer, he drew -- explained what he meant. We've always been neighbours but we've never been brothers. Hasn't the question been answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I put to you that if that sort of view, that you can't live together as brothers or as -- as neighbours, rather -- only as neighbours but not as brothers, rather, demonstrates a antipathy towards Bosnian Muslims and that might have reflected itself in your report when you deal with the suffering of Serbs and genocide against Serbs -- when you comment on the genocide against the Serbs in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is your free conclusion, but I disagree with it. I lived with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina since I was born. I worked in areas that were populated by Muslims, and we never had problems with them. However, the war brought about some new relations. There was a war which was a civil war, an inter-ethnic war, a religious war, and these relations changed profoundly. And it's possible that I gave an interview to this news agency in this context. But I disagree with you drawing free conclusions from that and attributing them to me, because I think that I am the one who can interpret my thoughts best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a public personality, and you can check my positions and my activities of today and my former activities. I have never had such undertones in my activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, okay, for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I would seek to tender that extract into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- the question is put to the witness and the witness has answered. Why do we need this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. I'll proceed. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 20087.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you just look at that particular article, Professor Pasalic. That's an article again obtained from the Internet, from a newspaper called -- or a publication or a media source called Glas, dated 10 May 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I submit that we should use the same methodology that Judge Hall suggested to the Prosecutor, that he pose a concrete question to the witness based on this text. We're not opposed to this text being used, but I think that a clear question should be put. I believe this is how we have proceeded so far, and we should be consistent in our approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to have a look at it, Professor Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it attributes words to you in the second -- second and third paragraphs. Are those words accurately reported? Did you say those words or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mostly correct. It's a result of my research and other research. The Serbs had the greatest number of victims in Sarajevo, and this text points this out once more. Since, in the research of Mirsad Tokaca, this was diminished greatly. I can show that on the example of other municipalities. Mr. Tokaca and I had a dialogue in the media about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information from my biography, and it is not contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. So look at the third paragraph, and you say there that -- you complain there that someone would give themselves an exclusive right to establish the exact number of victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of their nationality. And you complain, and I assume about Tokaca, filing the deaths of Serbs in Sarajevo under the category of political bargaining. You then go on to say that the data gathered by Tokaca and his centre minimises the number of Serb victims, and that's why Serbs don't trust his institution. And you complain of speculation about the number of Serb victims. You were, therefore, expressing publicly the view that the number of Serb victims was being diminished as a result of political bargaining by another demographic institution; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that I had major objections in relation to the research conducted by Mirsad Tokaca's centre, a centre as regards Serb victims in Sarajevo as well. Because his centre came to a symbolical number of victims. I cannot recall the exact figure. Now I think it was about 800 victims. And he kept that within the bounds of political bargaining, which I criticised. And then I showed him another example outside Sarajevo, indicating that that information is not correct. I took the example of the municipality of Zavidovici because I know it best, as I lived there myself, had lived there myself. Then we're going to compare that to Sarajevo. In Mr. Tokaca's report, it says that Zavidovici had a total of 890 victims of all ethnic backgrounds out of which 600 were Bosniaks. I documented that through a source, a book actually, that was published by the Zavidovici municipality. It is entitled "Life Without an End." And it includes documentation about those 600 Bosniaks. There is about 200 Croats victims because in 1993 in the territory of Zavidovici there was a direct war conflict between Bosniaks - Muslims, as they were called at the time - and Croats. And it turns out that there were only about 100 victims of Serb ethnicity. However, I provided data showing that only in the area of Vozuce there were about 400 victims. Some are still missing actually. Then the area of Dolac; that is near Zavidovici. And then the area of Bocinja. In the media and beyond the media that is a well-known area because of the Mujahedin. This shows that the number of Serb victims was minimised. This was just an example of this particular municipality. There are many municipalities that can be taken as such an example. On the basis of that, I proved that the structure of victims, according to ethnic background, in Mirsad Tokaca's report is incorrect. Why did the Serbs not trust that institution? Precisely because researchers on the ground, for the most part, and actually you can see that on the Internet, too, because that data was accessible to the public, they mostly represented the suffering and victimisation of ethnic Bosniaks, and this led to a lack of trust on the part of Serbs who lost some of their family members during the war, and therefore they did not report their losses to that institution. Also, it is impossible to report all Serb victims because many families were totally destroyed. There was no one left. No living person was left to report the losses. Or entire families moved out of the territory of the former Yugoslavia and there was no way in which these victims could have had been reported. This is incontrovertible evidence, and Mr. Tokaca ultimately agreed with me on that too, when we had this dialogue on TV once, although before that we had a media dialogue which was a bit more vociferous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a dispute with Mr. Tokaca about demographics figures concerning minimization of Serb deaths. The way you dealt with it was to go to the papers or deal with the issue through the media. Did you consider perhaps dealing with the issue through demographic journals, writing a scientific article and perhaps having it published, dealing with the issue in that way, this demographic issue in that manner, rather than making statements to the press? Because I suggest to you that would have been the hallmark of a dispassionate academic, dealing with numbers.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I did not initiate our dialogue through the media. That dialogue was initiated by Mr. Tokaca, as he presented this information in public. He made presentations of this data throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had these presentations, and we attended them directly or indirectly. It was advisable to take part in such discussions, especially from the point of view of a different standpoint. As for a scientific approach to this problem, in the bibliography there, you have my papers that I presented at scientific gatherings, where I, indeed, dealt with these matters, especially after the war. Since there was a shortage of papers on that subject, they drew a great deal of attention within Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. I always made an effort to present hard data, not something superficial or partial. Finally, over all these years, the objective of my research has been to get a comprehensive and realistic picture of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina without any minimizing or exaggeration in favour or against any ethnic group. I can say in all sincerity that I was never the object of critical attacks, because I carefully selected topics of research regarding things that I was sure of. If I'm not certain of something, I don't want to present that to the public or to an academic audience because this would be lacking in seriousness on anyone's part, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 20090.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the article is -- you can see in the B/C/S it's on the left-hand side. Okay. Could you just cast your eyes over that particular article. This is an article that appears to be from Oslobodjenje from the 26th of August, 2008, with the headline being "Pasalic: Bosniaks Want a Bosnian Nation."

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my interview to Oslobodjenje of Sarajevo. May I say, by the way, that in the Federation and in Republika Srpska it was very well received. I wish I had -- I wish you had the entire interview here. I speak about the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the media asked me about this as a demographer. So you see how journalists make mistakes. It says here, Professor, the Faculty of Philosophy in Banja Luka. That is not something I am. You see, that is a mistake on the part of the journalist, but I don't really --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, I cut you off. Please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do wish to provide my comments with regard to this article. You asked me about that. Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... good, so it's correct. In the second paragraph, you say: "He," that's you, "presumes that behind the idea not to register the ethnicity and religion of peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina there is a hidden intention to abolish the Serbian and Croatian national identity and ... create a 'Bosnian' nation." This all comes from whether or not questions in a proposed census should include questions about ethnicity and religion; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you will allow me to elaborate on this topic more extensively from a professional point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I don't want to go into the proposed form of the census. If there's any clarification, Mr. Cvijetic can do that. I want to ask you about the comment that you made about a hidden intention to abolish Serbian and Croatian national identity and create a Bosnian nation. Does -- why in particular did you make that comment?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I wish to explain. According to the principles and recommendations of the United Nations department - and they are accepted by Eurostat in Europe; this was recommended to all countries with regard to population censuses - in all multi-ethnic countries in Europe, in the census of 2001 about 70 per cent of countries had this question about national affiliation, linguistic, and religious affiliation, which is quite acceptable for multi-ethnic countries, and Bosnia-Herzegovina is one of them. After all, its constitution says that it is a state of three constituent peoples. What could you conclude then if the representatives, the political representatives, of one ethnic group or people do not wish to see that question in the census? I presented that as a hypothesis then, that this might mean that in the coming period there was an aspiration for establishing a so-called Bosnian nation. Among the Bosniak people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such aspirations are not totally foreign. They are not hidden. They are shown in public quite often. The very fact that one says Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat, et cetera, which is wrong, which is a wrong way of stating ethnic affiliation. That may indicate that too. So the census problem became a political problem. It is only the Bosniak political representatives still do not accept to have the census carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina primarily because of this ethnic, linguistic, and religious affiliation that is one of the questions. If we stick to our line of work, we have to be visionaries. We should not only deal with the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to project the future. So please view my statement in that context. And it's absolutely acceptable --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the end of the article you -- you express a fear that the Serbs -- that it's -- sorry. You express a fear that there's an endeavour underway to turn Serbs and Croats into Bosniaks. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what was carried in Oslobodjenje verbatim, I'm not denying it. I explained it very nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the name of a language, it is not based on a toponym. A toponym is a name for a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is the name of the people that should be reflected in the name of the language, the people speaking that language, not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. I know what a toponym is. Thanks. You don't need to explain it. The expressed fear in a newspaper -- in the -- in the media that there are measures afoot to turn Serbs and Croats into Bosniaks indicates that you've, as far as ethnic harmony is concerned in Bosnia, you hold very strong views, and you expressed them to the media. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a matter of argument. I think that the witness has already answered this question three times, the question put by my colleague Mr. Di Fazio. And now he is making an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me approach it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You deal with these issues by going to the media and complaining about the leadership of the two other ethnic groups and what they're -- and what they want to do, namely the transformation of Serbs and Croats into Bosniaks. You certainly don't deal with it by writing scholarly articles or academic articles, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot write academic articles in the media. You have to adapt your statements to what the media are asking you about. The media deal with daily events, political events, and so on. In such situations, for example, when you have this problem of the census in BH, the media talked to experts as well, as a rule. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is mostly those who deal with this particular subject, so demographers. I don't see anything that would be in dispute. The creation of a Bosnian nation was not something that happening during history, the creation of a Yugoslav nation proved to be impossible, so all the ethnic groups or nations wished to keep their national identity. That does not meant that that should lead to difference connotations, to conflicts, et cetera. So even the multi-ethnicity of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be pointed out as an advantage, as something that would show the harmony of the peoples within that community. That would clearly indicate what would happen if there would not be a question regarding ethnic affiliation in the census. How would the three constitute peoples be represented statistically after that in some other documents, and so on and so forth? That is where the political problem came into being. Why would that be a problem, having the census reflect the multi-ethnicity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a positive characteristic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? It should never be viewed as a negative characteristic. Those who oppose that question in the census are actually presenting the multi-ethnicity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a problem here. So when something is read in the newspapers, one has to know how to read between the lines, as it were, especially professional subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I think I can wrap this up by -- with one last question. This is what I suggest to you, put to you: You're a person who's quite comfortable with using statistics relating to the various ethnic groups in Bosnia, in the political sphere, and in the media. You're quite comfortable with that, I suggest. And shouldn't that cause concerns for the delivery of a dry -- sorry, for the delivery of a dispassionate, dry report dealing with demographic movements during the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. That is your free conclusion, and a wrong one at that. All the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both in the Federation and Republika Srpska, absolutely use interviews with me to clarify certain matters, in a professional way. If it were not so, then probably some media would no longer cooperate with me. I never abuse statistics for such purposes. But as a public person, it is my duty to provide certain interpretations to the media and to the general public. That does not mean that everyone necessarily has to agree with what I say. But if we are talking about professional matters, about science, then you have to present hard facts. There is no compromise there. I repeat, compromise is only made in politics, and I'm not making any statements here as a politician. I'm helping resolve some political issues by relying on my profession. The population census in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a way for us to help register the entire population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is something that is absolutely needed by all in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, that's the end of my cross-examination. I just want to remind you that I will be seeking to tender the excerpt from the book headed "Anthropogeographic Reality of Serbs." That's 65 ter 20081. It's the introduction to his book and the corresponding B/C/S pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How many pages do you seek to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's -- I don't know the exact total, but I can let you know in just a moment, if Your Honours will give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Six pages, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As Your Honours can see, I'm replacing Mr. Hannis for the last session so I can deal with the matter arising out of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this will be a quick and easy one. I have no questions for Professor Pasalic for re-examination. I just would like to express my gratitude for -- to him for being able to summon enough energy to come here and testify. The only thing I do have is move to tender his report, together with the annexes, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we deal with this after the witness is -- has left, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Professor, paragraph 75 of your report mentions the March 1992 referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the fact that the West accepted the outcome of the referendum as the basis for the creation of a new state. These are two facts. The paragraph continues: "However, a consensus of the three constituent people was the most rational solution bearing in mind the fact that none of the peoples was the majority." Do you see that? My question --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The consensus being a more rational solution, is that a fact as well or is that an opinion ? And if it is, as I presume, an opinion, is that an opinion that falls within the scope of your expertise as a demographer?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was my opinion then and it is still my opinion that the consensus of the three constituent peoples is required in Bosnia-Herzegovina for all issues. And then, as we say proverbially in my country, we'll have a peaceful Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But my question is: Is that a personal opinion or is that an expert opinion? Is that your opinion based on demography?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my opinion that is not directly related to demography. I state it in my introduction to the monograph about "The Anthropogenic Reality of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina." This is a free opinion of mine that need not be connected with demography. But then the question is: What is not interlinked in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including demography?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In paragraph 7, that is, in the introduction, you state that the aim of your report is to present the scope of demographic changes caused by the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to paragraph 78, the territorial scope of your research is the territories inhabited by the Serbian population and this is as opposed to areas controlled by Muslim and Croat forces, since you had no possibility to research the events in these areas, and you explained that to a certain extent. My question is this: Is that a scientifically valid equation of mutually exclusive concepts, that is, territories inhabited by the Serbian population, as opposed to areas controlled by Muslim and Croat forces during the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A scientific approach could have encompassed the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, certainly if the preconditions are met. But it can also research a part of its territory, irrespective of which ethnic group is dominant there. My goal was to amend or complement numerous other studies for all these together to become a more realistic reflection of the processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war. I didn't aspire to, nor did I have the capacity to, conduct a research that would encompass all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't believe that there are such individuals there even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry to interrupt you, but I think you don't understand my question. Territories controlled by the Muslim and Croat forces, are -- are that -- are they, by definition, territories that are not inhabited by Serb population, or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the wartime period, and there was a symbolic presence of Serbs in these areas, taking into account the fact that immediately before the armed conflict or during the armed conflict they were expelled. Not all areas were directly affected by armed conflict during the war, but the indirect consequences could be felt nonetheless. Croatian Muslim forces controlled certain areas where the Serb population then was reduced to a minimum. And even now their numbers are very small. I have already pointed out that the share of the Serbs in the population of the Federation is up to 4 per cent, and that is clearly a consequence of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, then. In the territories you could do your research in, the ones with Serb population that was not under control of the Muslim and Croat forces during the war, you explored, according to paragraph 79, and the fifth conclusion of your report: "The war influenced or forced migrations of Serbs." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have explained in my evidence that I researched the demographic processes, most of all migrations, which during a war are, by necessity, forced. But we classified them into several subgroups I don't need to repeat. But I focussed on the forced migrations of the Serb population, and I explained the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Back for a moment to the two categories of territories, the ones you could do your research on and the ones you couldn't, the Serb-controlled ones and the ones controlled by the Muslim and the Croat forces. In what category would you place, generally speaking, without going into detail, the municipalities in the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember these municipalities, some of them were controlled by different sides at different points in time, others were not. And today five municipalities are in the Federation, and others are in Republika Srpska. For example, Kljuc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, no, just during the war. Is there a majority of them -- of these municipalities that were in this category or in the other one?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of these municipalities were controlled by the Serb forces, and that is why I put forward the -- the argument that this is a badly chosen sample because it gives a wrong picture of what was happening during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so basically --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But some municipalities did -- did pass to the control of the other side during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But basically they were municipalities, Serb-populated municipalities, as you call them, in categorising the two? That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would now have to take the document and precisely interpret the share of individual ethnic groups in those municipalities because I don't want to speak from memory and in general terms. In that way, we could see where the Serbs or Muslims or possibly Croats, but they weren't the majority anywhere, possibly the relative majority, in some places. My remark was that the selection of municipalities wasn't the best, if we want to get a faithful reflection of the processes. This selection of municipalities gives a distorted picture. If we were to take other municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's not the purpose my question, excuse me. I go back to paragraph 79 of your report and the fifth conclusion of it, in which you say that you researched on the war-influenced or forced migration of the Serbs within the Serb-populated territories. And the only reference to, or conclusion, about the war-influenced migrations of the other ethnic groups that one finds in your report is that the forced migration of the Serb population led to or brought about the same forced migrations of other ethnic groups. That is what I read in paragraph 75 and in the fifth conclusion of your report. And for that reason, you say, the aim of your report is to point to, to underline, the complexity of the migration of the population in these territories during the 1992-1995 war, in particular. Is that a fair summary of the fifth conclusion of your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I need some time to find it. You say conclusion number 5. I cannot seem to -- because the conclusion 5 is something else in -- in my report. "The territory of BH is characterised by very complex historical" -- no, that's the introduction. I apologise. I'm still looking for the fifth conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist, these are your final conclusions, Professor, on page 71 in your version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it reads: "The study of the Serbian war -- "The study of the Serbian war migrations or war-forced migrations and their causes and consequences for this report led to the war-forced migrations of other ethnic groups. For this reason, this report aims to point to the complexity of the migration of the population in this territory throughout history and the 1992-1995 war, in particular." That's what I was citing; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The point of this report is that what we metaphorically called connected vessels or a chain reaction or the flow and counterflow of migrational movements, and migrations in wartime are, generally speaking, forced. But this was mostly about the transfer of population that moved toward ethnically dominate areas, which I qualified as a process of ethnic and territorial homogenisation. And I believe that that's what these data point to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now my next question is this: If you would have been asked to do so, could you have explored in your report for those same territories the war-influenced or forced migration of the non-Serb population? Would you have been able to do that, if asked?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the war because it would have been impossible physically. We spoke about that movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the post-war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You were asked in 2011 to write this report, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about this, yes. I would be willing to conduct research in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Only I'm not sure if I know that part of the territory so well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not speaking about the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm talking about the territories you [indiscernible] strong in this -- in -- in this report now, the Serb-populated territories, and I'm talking about -- the question is in -- would you have been able to examine, if asked, the war-influenced migration of the non-Serb in these same territories?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I think I would be less well acquainted with this material. But, as a member of a team of experts, I would be able to do such research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I -- I take it you have not been asked to do that research.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I haven't been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the territories you did your research in, that is, the Serb-populated territories -- No, the qualification the expert gave is Serb-populated. So -- and it was your own choice to focus in this report on the Serb migration, Serb war-influenced migrations within these territories.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Now I understand. In this report, I didn't have the capability to conduct research in other territories in a short time-period. But I said yesterday, or the other day, that Ewa Tabeau did that with her co-workers and that would have been a repetition of the numerical indicators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking about. Aren't you more or less saying that you have no real expert knowledge of the migration of the non-Serb population in the Serb-populated territories in general or in the indictment municipalities in particular?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had -- have no expert knowledge. But we haven't shaped our knowledge into a report. But knowing the processes -- knowledge of the processes, especially the migrations during the war in BiH, is present in both me and other researchers. However, we weren't able to conduct such research for reasons of time and other reasons I mentioned. I personally considered that Ewa Tabeau's comprehensive research into this opened the door to additional research, which may be subject to criticism, but it is complementary to hers. And I think that the value of both reports is that together they give a more complete and clearer picture, rather than overlapping and describing this -- the same situation or processes and phenomena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you say that the knowledge that you had about the non-Serb migration, you didn't -- you haven't shaped your knowledge into this report. Isn't that an odd choice, given the fact that this trial is not about forced migration of Serb population but, among other things, forced migration about non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the non-Serb population. But my position was, if -- if we add to this report the problems connected to the forced migrations of the Serb population, only then can we have a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon and processes in the area, without which a historically distorted picture would be created or we could also speak about the bias of statistical data used in other reports. And I still continue to stress the necessity to research the forced migrations of all population groups because that -- these processes are interconnected. The phrase "connected vessels" has been used here, and it was not easy to control these things by any means. We're talking about some 4 million-odd people who were involved in these processes, which is very complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Professor, we thank you for your attendance before the Tribunal. Your testimony is now at an end, and you're now released. We wish you a safe journey back to your home. The usher will escort you from the courtroom. The Court has over matters with which to deal before it rises.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I do want to raise a matter with the Chamber concerning the report, if now would be an appropriate time. And I can keep it very, very brief. I'm mindful -- I know that the Prosecution did not object to the expertise of Professor Pasalic or indeed the relevance of his report, and I'm mindful of the President's question to me about expertise. I bear all of that in mind. However, I think that it is appropriate for the Prosecution to register its objection to the relevance and the expertise of Professor Pasalic, having heard all of his evidence over the last three days. Just insofar as his expertise is concerned, and, of course, we don't object to his doubt of expertise in social geography, but, in my submission, the cross-examination on his expertise on Tuesday is such that such serious doubts have been raised about it that you should rule against him as an expert. That's all I want to say about that, and I'm mindful, of course, it's a decision for Your Honours. On the other issue of relevance, however, I also want to register an objection to the admission of the report. It's -- it was always clear that the report only ever dealt with Serbian population movements, but the Prosecution thought that it might somehow, the provision of the testimony, it might -- the relevance to the other two ethnic groups might somehow be explained. That hasn't happened over the last three days, in the Prosecution's submission, and it's pretty clear that he, just from what happened this morning, that he is less well acquainted with war-influenced migrations of non-Serbs. And I think he effectively said this morning that he didn't have sufficient expert knowledge of non-Serb populated territories. In addition to that, everything that he said over the last three days, in the Prosecution's submission, really can only apply to the movements of Serbs and not the other two ethnic groups --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, as you develop this, Mr. Di Fazio, what do you make of the witness's statement that he repeated several time in cross-examination in particular - I can't remember if it came up in examination-in-chief - that his report should be regarded as being complementary to the other reports that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think it's complementary. It can only focus on one ethnic group. I thought that it would somehow shed light on the movements of the other ethnic groups, but it doesn't. It can only be confined to the migratory movements of Serbs and not the other two groups, so it doesn't complement Ewa Tabeau's reports, in my submission. It doesn't add anything further, any significant or important further evidence or information to the material that she presented to you. So it's got to the point, in the Prosecution's submission, where the relevance is simply gone -- is simply so minimal and so peripheral that it really can't find its way into the trial record. And so for those reasons, it should be -- should be -- it shouldn't be admitted. May I just confer with my colleague, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Ms. Korner makes the point that it is also blemished by the fact that's essentially a tu quoque report. And that's apparent from the annexes. You recall, the annexes only -- in particular, Annex B -- Annex A only deals with, in the broadest of terms, with Serb execution sites, Serb expulsions, and Serb -- and the destruction of Serb property, Serb town and villages. So as it's developed over the last three days, the Prosecution says that the relevance of the report has been demonstrated to be so minimal that it simply doesn't make the grade and shouldn't be admitted. However, that's -- of course, we realize it is entirely a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to explain the reasons and motives for the engagement of the demographer Professor Stevo Pasalic by the Defence to write such a paper. We did not want to negate in an absolute sense the findings of Ms. Ewa Tabeau. The objections to the methodological approach and some possible errors and omissions that may be a result of such a -- such an approach were presented by Professor Stevo Pasalic. However, he did not negate her report as a whole. Had we done that, it would have been our duty to do what Judge Delvoie mentioned, to make an effort and to present a different report and to invest ten years in that. That is not what we did. Your Honours, we wanted to expand the factual basis of the evidence in terms of ethnodemographic trends in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the segment in which we believe that the paper of Ms. Ewa Tabeau did not provide answers. In that complex mosaic of ethnodemographic trends, we believe that the professor provided just one tile, but a very useful one. We're not saying that he responded to each and every question, nor was he in a position to do so. However, the Trial Chamber, as they see both reports before them, will have a broader basis to rely on what you consider to be useful for this case and for reaching your decision ultimately. So if you assess both papers, the two together are of greater value than any one of the two individually. Two experts know more than one. We will have a great deal more scope for argumentation, we and the Prosecution. And ultimately, you will have a bigger basis for your own decision. Probably we did not manage to produce everything that we wanted to, but I'm sure that I can safely say that we have more before us now than if we only had Ms. Tabeau's report. Please understand the witness in that way, complementary in that sense. Complementary in that part in which the paper did not provide some of the key answers that we believe were necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Mr. Krgovic, do you wish to be heard on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. That was joint submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank counsel for their submissions. The Chamber will decide on the application for the admission of the report of Professor Pasalic sometime next week, we trust. There is a question that I have of the parties, in terms of next week. But before I do that, there's a ruling that we have to deliver which may affect the question I'm about to ask. And the ruling is as follows. The Trial Chamber is seized of an oral application raised by the Stanisic Defence on the 13th of April, 2011, seeking sanctions against the Prosecution under Rule 68 bis of the rules for alleged non-disclosure of documents relating to the witness who is to return next week for further cross-examination. That is an Andrija Bjelosevic. The Defence alleges that the Prosecution has not disclosed to it, among other things, documents that relate to a Prosecution interview with the witness which were -- are said to be subject to disclosure under Rule 66(B) and which appeared on the Prosecution list of documents to be used in cross-examination of the witness released by the Prosecution on the 12th of April, 2011, at the start of his testimony, as required by the procedural guide-lines issued by the Chamber. The Chamber has heard oral submissions from all parties on the matter on a number of occasions, in particular on the 14th and 21st of April, and on the 2nd and 5th of May.
